links.note: 1001 calls the man who stores up great wealth and does not use it dead (செத்தான்); 214 says whoever does not know and do what is fitting (ஒத்தது அறிவான்) is 'placed among the dead' (செத்தாருள் வைக்கப்படும்). Both use death as a verdict on a living person, once for failing to use wealth and once for failing in ஒப்புரவு, so the hoarder falls under both.

229 says eating alone in order to fill up one's store (நிரப்பிய தாமே தமியர் உணல்) is more bitter than begging; 1001 takes the case one step further, the man who does not even eat it (அஃதுண்ணான்), and calls him dead. Read together they grade the misuse of wealth: unshared use is wretched, no use at all is not living.

The two verses end with the same line, மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு. In 351 the delusion (மருள்) is taking what is not real for real (பொருளல்லவற்றைப் பொருளென்று); in 1002 it is holding that everything comes by wealth (பொருளானாம் எல்லாம்) and so clinging without giving. The pairing shows the miser's belief treated as a case of the same error about பொருள், with the same result in birth; Parimelazhagar glosses the birth in 1002 as a ghost's and in 351 as a joyless one.

751 says nothing but wealth makes people of no account into people of account (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). 1002 names nearly the same thought, பொருளானாம் எல்லாம், as what the miser thinks, and says that when it leads to not giving (ஈயாது இவறும்) it is delusion. The chapter on making wealth is thus limited here: the claim holds only for wealth that is given and used.

Both end in நிலக்குப் பொறை, a burden to the earth: in 572 it is the existence (உண்மை) of those without kindly regard, in 1003 the appearance (தோற்றம்) of men who cling to accumulation and do not want renown (இசை வேண்டா). The same sentence is passed on two kinds of people who are of no use to others.

239 says land that bears a body without renown (இசையிலா யாக்கை பொறுத்த நிலம்) declines in its yield; 1003 says those who hoard and do not want இசை are a burden to the land. 239 states a consequence for the land of the weight 1003 names, and both rest on பொறு, the earth's bearing.

236 says: if you appear, appear with renown; for those without it not appearing is better (தோன்றலின் தோன்றாமை நன்று). 1003 calls the தோற்றம் of hoarders who do not want renown a burden to the earth, and Manakkudavar reads it as saying it is better they were not born. The chapter on useless wealth applies the rule of the chapter on renown to the miser.

238 calls renown the legacy (இசையென்னும் எச்சம்) and says failing to get it is a reproach. 1004 asks what the man wanted by no one (நச்சப்படாதவன்) supposes his எச்சம் will be. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 1004, renown stays only with the giver, so the question applies 238 to the miser and finds he has nothing to leave.

114 says whether people were worthy or not is seen from their எச்சம்; 1004 asks what எச்சம் the unwanted man imagines for himself. Parimelazhagar takes the word as offspring in 114 and as what remains after death, i.e. renown, in 1004, so the pairing shows the same test of a life by what it leaves, applied with two senses of the word.

89 defines poverty in the midst of having (உடைமையுள் இன்மை) as the folly of neglecting guests; 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with piled-up crores (கோடி உண்டாயினும் இல்). Both say that possession without giving counts as not having, once in the household setting and once for wealth at large.

377 says even those who have amassed crores cannot enjoy them except as the apportioner has apportioned (கோடி தொகுத்தார்க்கும் துய்த்தல் அரிது). 1005 treats not enjoying and not giving (கொடுப்பதூஉம் துய்ப்பதூஉம் இல்லார்) as the person's own lack. The chapter on fate adds that the failure to enjoy one's crores may not be wholly in one's hands, which limits how far 1005's judgment can be read as blame.

430 says those without understanding have nothing, whatever they have (என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்); 1005 says the same of those who neither give nor enjoy, even with crores. The same form of argument, that owning is not having unless some further quality is present, is used for understanding in one place and for use and giving in the other.

212 says all wealth won by effort is for doing வேளாண்மை, with தக்கார் in the picture (Parimelazhagar takes it as wealth of the worthy owner, others as help to the worthy). 1006 describes the man who does not use his wealth and has no habit of giving to the deserving (தக்கார்க்கொன்று ஈதல் இயல்பிலாதான்) as ஏதம் to great wealth. 212 gives the purpose of wealth and 1006 the case where that purpose is defeated; Parimelazhagar says the man is a disease to the wealth because he makes it not what it is for.

1000 says great wealth got by a man without courtesy is like good milk turned by the fault of its vessel (கலந்தீமையால் திரிந்தற்று); 1006 says the man who neither uses nor gives is ஏதம் to பெருஞ்செல்வம். In both the wealth is good in itself and the holder is what spoils it, which is how Parimelazhagar reads 1006 (others take the wealth to be a misery to him).

226 says ending the ruinous hunger of the destitute (அற்றார் அழிபசி தீர்த்தல்) is the place where one who has got wealth stores it. 1007 says the wealth of one who does nothing for the destitute (அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான்) is like a very beautiful woman growing old alone. 226 says where wealth is kept safe; 1007 shows what happens to wealth kept anywhere else: it passes its time unused.

1039 says land whose owner stays away sulks like a wife (இல்லாளின் ஊடிவிடும்); 1007 likens ungiven wealth to a beautiful woman who ages alone (தமியள் மூத்தற்று). Both picture a good left unattended as a woman without her partner, for farmland in one verse and for money in the other; Parimelazhagar notes for 1007 that the wealth itself loses its fruit.

216 says wealth with a man of நயன் is like a fruit tree ripening in the middle of the town (பயன்மரம் உள்ளூர்ப் பழுத்தற்று); 1008 says the wealth of the man no one wants is a poison tree ripening in the middle of the town (நடுவூருள் நச்சுமரம் பழுத்தற்று). The image is the same and only the tree differs, so the two verses read as a deliberate pair: the place and the ripeness are equal, and the owner decides whether anyone can eat.

760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in plenty (ஒண்பொருள் காழ்ப்ப இயற்றியார்க்கு) the other two, virtue and pleasure, come easily. 1009 uses the same word, ஒண்பொருள், for wealth amassed by dropping love, denying oneself and not looking to virtue, and says others will take it. So the promise of 760 fails when the two ends it names are given up in the earning; Parimelazhagar reads 760 as wealth that comes by the right way.

755 says wealth-making that does not come with அருள் and அன்பு should be let go; 1009 says wealth gathered by abandoning அன்பு and ignoring அறம் ends with others. The first gives the rule in the chapter on making wealth, and the second gives the outcome when the rule is ignored.

837 says that when a fool gets great wealth, strangers are filled and his own people go hungry (ஏதிலார் ஆரத் தமர் பசிப்பர்); 1009 says the miser's wealth is taken by others (கொள்வார் பிறர்), which Parimelazhagar reads as not even reaching his own line. Folly and miserliness arrive at the same result by opposite routes, one by careless spending and one by spending nothing.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, 1010 says the brief want (சிறுதுனி) of the rich who have renown is like the rain cloud running dry (மாரி வறங்கூர்ந்தனையது). 219 says the poverty of a man of நயன் is just his not being able to do what he is used to doing. Both treat the giver's poverty as a loss to others, not to himself, and 1010 adds by its image that it passes.

211 uses மாரி as the model of giving that asks no return; 1010 uses மாரி for the renowned rich in a lean spell. The same figure is carried from the chapter on ஒப்புரவு into the chapter on useless wealth, where it marks by contrast what the miser's wealth never is.

Manakkudavar reads 1010 differently: the renowned rich, in a small displeasure (சிறுதுனி), not giving is like the rains failing. On that reading 17 is the fuller statement of the image: even the sea loses its nature if the cloud takes from it and does not give back (எழிலி தான் நல்காதாகி விடின்). The link depends on Manakkudavar's reading and not on Parimelazhagar's.

201 says the excellent fear the intoxication called evil deed (விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்); 1011 defines shame proper as shame on account of deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்). Fear and shame are given the same object, one's own wrong action, in two chapters, and Parimelazhagar glosses நாணுதல் elsewhere (433, 172) as அஞ்சுதல்.

1011 sets aside the modesty of bright-browed women (திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாணு) as something other than the shame it means. 907 says a woman who has shame (நாணுடைப் பெண்) has more greatness than the manhood of one who does a woman's bidding, which Parimelazhagar glosses as a man without shame. So the shame 1011 puts second is still ranked above a man's lack of the first kind.

1011 mentions the other shame, that of women, without describing it. In 1251 a woman in the Book of Love describes it from inside: shame is the bolt (நாணுத்தாழ்) on the door of her restraint, which the axe of desire breaks. This is a speech in character, but it shows what the shame 1011 calls பிற is: a guard on conduct in love, not a recoil from a wrong deed.

972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction differs by the work they do (பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் சிறப்பொவ்வா); 1012 says food, clothing and the rest are no different for all beings and the distinction of people is having shame (உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல ... மாந்தர் சிறப்பு). Both have the form 'common to all, சிறப்பு from one thing', and they name different things: deeds in one, shame in the other.

993 says likeness of limbs is not likeness among people; the likeness that counts is of character (பண்பொத்தல்). 1012 says the bodily needs are shared by all and shame is what sets people apart. Both refuse to take what is physically common as the measure of a human being.

410 says the unlearned stand to the learned as beasts stand to people; 1012 says what all beings share is food and clothing and what marks people is shame. Each chapter claims its own quality as the line that divides the human from the rest, learning in 410 and shame in 1012.

983 lists shame (நாண்) as one of five pillars that hold up சால்பு, with love, ஒப்புரவு, kindly regard and truthfulness. 1013 says சால்பு is fixed on the good called shame as all lives are fixed on the body (ஊனைக் குறித்த உயிரெல்லாம்). The chapter on shame makes one of the five the seat of the whole; Manakkudavar says other qualities are needed but this one cannot be done without.

80 says the seat of life goes by way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை) and without it a body is bones wrapped in skin; 1013 says worth depends on shame as life depends on flesh. Both use the life-and-body relation to say a quality is what a thing lives by, love for the person in 80 and shame for சால்பு in 1013. Parimelazhagar notes a variant ஊணை ('food') in 1013, which Manakkudavar follows; the link rests on the reading ஊனை.

Both verses turn on பீடு நடை, the proud walk. 59 says those whose home does not seek renown cannot walk it before people who scorn them; 1014 says that for the worthy without shame the proud walk is a disease (பிணி), which Parimelazhagar takes as painful to those who see it. The gait is earned by something behind it, the household's good name in one verse and shame in the other.

575 says kindly regard is the eye's ornament and without it the eye is known as a sore (அணிகலம் ... அஃதின்றேல் புண்); 1014 says shame is the ornament of the worthy and without it the proud walk is a disease (அணி ... அஃதின்றேல் பிணி). The two share one construction: a thing without its ornament is not plain but a bodily affliction.

118 (with 115) calls not leaning to one side the ornament of the worthy (கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி); 1014 calls shame the ornament of the worthy (அணியன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு). The same phrase names two inner restraints, and neither is an outward decoration.

315 asks what understanding is worth if one does not guard against another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்); 1015 says the world calls those who are ashamed at others' disgrace and their own alike (பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும்) the home of shame. The move of treating another's case as one's own is made for pain in one verse and for disgrace in the other.

980 says greatness covers others' exposure (அற்றம் மறைக்கும்) and smallness only speaks their faults. 1015 gives the feeling behind that conduct: being ashamed of another's disgrace as of one's own. One who feels the other's பழி in this way has no reason to tell it.

1015 praises one who feels shame even for others' disgrace; 1018 describes one who does not feel shame at what makes others ashamed (பிறர் நாணத்தக்கது தான் நாணான்). The two set out the ends of a scale inside the chapter: shame that extends beyond oneself, and shame that fails even for one's own act.

311 says the spotless hold to not hurting others even if it would bring wealth that gives distinction. 1016, on Parimelazhagar's reading, says the high take shame as their fence and do not want the wide world (வியன்ஞாலம் பேணலர்) where the two conflict. Both state a refusal of great gain at the price of a restraint; the other reading he reports, that they will not want the world without first having the fence of shame, gives the same result.

57 says confinement does little to guard women and the guard kept by their own firmness (நிறைகாக்கும் காப்பு) is best; 1016 says the high have shame for their fence (நாண்வேலி). In both the effective guard is a quality inside the person and not an outer barrier, for a wife's fidelity in one and for the conduct of the high in the other.

421 calls understanding an inner fortress enemies cannot destroy (உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்); 1016 calls shame a fence (வேலி), which Parimelazhagar explains as keeping blame and sin from entering. Both give an inner quality the work of a defensive structure, one against ruin and one against disgrace.

969 says those like the yak that will not live once its hair is lost give up life when honour is at stake (உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்); 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and not shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). The chapters on honour and shame make the same ranking of life below the quality, in adjoining parts of the book.

131 says conduct is to be guarded more than life (உயிரினும் ஓம்பப்படும்) because it gives excellence; 1017 says shame is not given up for the sake of life. The same comparison with life is used for conduct in the Book of Virtue and for shame here.

In 1132 a lover says his body and life, unable to bear more, will mount the palmyra horse after setting shame aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). 1017 says those ruled by shame will not give up shame for life's sake (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார்). The same choice between shame and life is posed in love and resolved the other way; this is a lover's speech in a chapter about abandoning shame, so it shows the pressure 1017 has in view and is not a rival teaching.

924 says Shame, the good woman, turns her back (நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும்) on the drinker; 1018 says that if a man is not ashamed of what shames others, it is a thing virtue would be ashamed of (அறம் நாணத்தக்கது), which Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read as virtue leaving or not approaching him. In both a personified quality withdraws from the shameless person, shame herself in one and virtue in the other.

130 says virtue watches for the right moment and comes by the path to the one who guards against anger and has learned restraint (அறம் பார்க்கும் ஆற்றின் நுழைந்து). 1018, as the commentators read it, has virtue ashamed to come near the shameless. Together they give the two directions of the same figure: virtue seeks out the restrained and shrinks from those without shame.

204 says that if one plots another's ruin, அறம் plots the plotter's ruin; 1018 says that if one is not ashamed, அறம் is ashamed. In both, virtue is an agent that answers the person's act in the terms of that act, with a penalty in 204 and with withdrawal in 1018.

960 says: if you want நலம், want shame; if you want குலம், want humility toward all. 1019 says a lapse in principle burns the குலம் and settled shamelessness burns the நலம். Both pair the same two goods and tie நலம் to shame, one as advice and one as warning; Parimelazhagar takes நலம் in 1019 to cover every good, from birth and learning to conduct.

133 says having conduct is good family and a lapse becomes low birth (இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்); the first half of 1019 says the same, that a lapse in கொள்கை burns the குலம். 1019 then sets shamelessness beside it as destroying more, and Parimelazhagar draws the conclusion that loss of shame is worse than loss of conduct.

952 says the well-born do not slip in three things: conduct, truthfulness and shame (ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும்). 1019 says what happens when two of those three fail: a lapse in conduct burns the family, and shamelessness that stays burns every good. The chapter on good family gives the mark and 1019 gives the cost of losing it.

Both use the wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை). In 1058 the wide world without anyone who asks would be puppets going and coming (சென்றுவந்தற்று); in 1020 the movement of those with no shame within is a puppet feigning life by its string (நாணால் உயிர் மருட்டியற்று). The image marks motion without what makes it human, which is giving and receiving in one verse and shame in the other; 1020 also plays on நாண், shame and string.

407 says the good looks of one without fine, penetrating understanding are those of a well-decorated clay doll (மண்மாண் புனைபாவை); 1020 says the shameless move like a wooden puppet. Both use a பாவை for a person who has the outward form without the inner quality, appearance without understanding in 407 and movement without shame in 1020.

80 says that without love a body is bones wrapped in skin; 1020 says that without shame within (நாண் அகத்தில்லார்) a person's movement is a puppet's and only imitates life. Each chapter names its quality as what makes a body a living person, and Manakkudavar reads 1020 as saying the shameless are not people.
